title: Chapter 14
paragraphs: Riding back to the house in the best of moods, Levin heard a bell ring at the side of the main entrance.

"That'll be someone from the train station," he thought. "Right about the time for the Moscow train to get in... Who could it be? What if it's my brother Nikolay? He did say: 'Maybe I'll go take the waters, or maybe I'll come stay with you.'" For a moment he felt uneasy and annoyed that his brother's arrival might disturb his happy spring mood. But he felt ashamed of the thought, and immediately, so to speak, opened his arms wide, and with a softened feeling of joy and anticipation, hoped with all his heart that it really was his brother. He spurred his horse on, and riding out from behind the acacia trees, he saw a hired three-horse sledge from the station, and a man in a fur coat. It wasn't his brother. "Oh, if only it were someone pleasant I could talk to a little!" he thought.
"Ah!" Levin cried joyfully, throwing up both hands. "What a wonderful guest! I'm so glad to see you!" he shouted, recognizing Stepan Arkadyevitch.
"I'll find out for certain whether she's married, or when she's going to be," he thought. And on that gorgeous spring day, he felt that even the thought of her didn't hurt at all.

"Well, you didn't expect me, did you?" said Stepan Arkadyevitch, climbing out of the sledge, mud splattered across the bridge of his nose, his cheek, and his eyebrows, but glowing with health and good spirits. "First of all, I came to see you," he said, hugging and kissing him, "second, to get some snipe shooting in, and third, to sell the forest at Ergushovo."
"Wonderful! What a spring we're having! How did you even manage in a sledge?"
"In a cart it would've been even worse, Konstantin Dmitrievitch," the driver, who knew him, answered.
"Well, I'm very, very glad to see you," Levin said, with a genuinely delighted, childlike smile.

Levin brought his friend to the guest room, where Stepan Arkadyevitch's things had also been carried — a bag, a gun case, a cigar pouch. Leaving him there to wash up and change, Levin went off to the estate office to talk about the ploughing and the clover. Agafea Mihalovna, always anxious about the household's reputation, met him in the hall with questions about dinner.
"Do whatever you like, just make it quick," he said, and went to find the bailiff.
When he came back, Stepan Arkadyevitch, washed and combed, emerged from his room with a beaming smile, and the two of them went upstairs together.

"Well, I'm glad I finally got away to visit you! Now I'll get to see what mysterious business keeps you so occupied out here. No, really, I envy you. What a house — everything about it is so nice! So bright, so cheerful!" said Stepan Arkadyevitch, forgetting that it wasn't always spring and fine weather like today. "And your housekeeper is simply delightful! A pretty maid in an apron might be a bit more fun, maybe, but for your monk-like way of living, she suits perfectly."
Stepan Arkadyevitch shared plenty of interesting news; Levin was especially interested to hear that his brother, Sergey Ivanovitch, was planning to visit him that summer.

Stepan Arkadyevitch didn't say a single word about Kitty or the Shtcherbatskys — only passed along greetings from his wife. Levin was grateful for his tact, and glad to have him as a guest. As always happened during his time alone, a mass of ideas and feelings had been piling up inside him that he'd had no one to share with. And now he poured it all out to Stepan Arkadyevitch — his poetic delight in the spring, his setbacks and plans for the land, his thoughts and criticisms of the books he'd been reading, and the idea for his own book, which was really — though he hadn't quite realized it himself — a critique of every old book ever written on agriculture. Stepan Arkadyevitch, always charming, picking up on everything with the slightest hint, was especially charming on this visit, and Levin noticed in him a kind of special warmth, a new note of respect that he found flattering.

Agafea Mihalovna and the cook worked hard to make dinner especially good, but their efforts only led to the two starving friends tearing through the starter course, eating heaps of bread and butter, salted goose, and pickled mushrooms — enough that Levin ended up ordering the soup served without the little pies the cook had particularly wanted to impress their guest with. But even though Stepan Arkadyevitch was used to very different meals, he found everything wonderful — the herb brandy, the bread, the butter, and above all the salted goose and mushrooms, the nettle soup, the chicken in white sauce, and the white Crimean wine. Every bit of it was superb and delicious.

"Splendid, splendid!" he said, lighting a fat cigar after the roast. "Coming out here feels like landing on a calm shore after the noise and shaking of a steamship. So you're saying the laborer himself is something to study, something that should shape the choice of methods in farming? Of course, I'm an ignorant outsider, but I'd guess theory and its application will end up shaping the laborer too."

"Yes, but wait a minute. I'm not talking about political economy — I'm talking about agricultural science. It should work like the natural sciences: observing the given facts, including the laborer, in his economic and ethnographic context..."
Just then Agafea Mihalovna came in with the jam.
"Oh, Agafea Mihalovna," said Stepan Arkadyevitch, kissing his plump fingertips, "what a goose, what brandy!... So, what do you think — time to head out, Kostya?" he added.
Levin looked out the window at the sun sinking behind the bare treetops of the forest.
"Yes, it's time," he said. "Kouzma, get the trap ready," and he ran downstairs.

On his way down, Stepan Arkadyevitch carefully took the canvas cover off his polished gun case with his own hands and, opening it, began preparing his expensive, latest-model gun. Kouzma, already smelling a good tip, never left Stepan Arkadyevitch's side, helping him on with both his stockings and boots — a job Stepan Arkadyevitch happily let him do.
"Kostya, tell them that if the merchant Ryabinin shows up... I told him to come today... he's to be brought in and told to wait for me..."
"Wait — you're selling the forest to Ryabinin?"
"Yes. Do you know him?"
"Of course I do. I've had to deal with him — 'positively and conclusively.'"
Stepan Arkadyevitch laughed. "Positively and conclusively" were the merchant's favorite words.
"Yes, it's incredibly funny how he talks. She knows exactly where her master's headed!" he added, patting Laska, who hovered around Levin, whining and licking his hands, his boots, and his gun.
The trap was already waiting at the steps when they came out.
"I had them bring the trap round — or would you rather walk?"

"No, let's drive," said Stepan Arkadyevitch, climbing into the trap. He sat down, tucked the tiger-skin rug around himself, and lit a cigar. "How do you not smoke? A cigar is a strange thing — not exactly pleasure itself, but the crowning proof of it. Now this is living! How wonderful! This is how I'd love to live!"
"Well, who's stopping you?" said Levin, smiling.
"No, you're the lucky one! You've got everything you want. You like horses — you have them; dogs — you have them; hunting — you have it; farming — you have it."
"Maybe it's because I enjoy what I have instead of pining for what I don't," Levin said, thinking of Kitty.
Stepan Arkadyevitch understood, glanced at him, but said nothing.

Levin was grateful to Oblonsky for noticing, with his usual tact, that Levin dreaded any talk of the Shtcherbatskys, and for saying nothing about them. But now Levin was desperate to find out what was troubling him so much, and yet he couldn't work up the nerve to ask.
"Come on, tell me how things are going with you," Levin said, realizing it wasn't fair of him to think only about himself.
Stepan Arkadyevitch's eyes lit up cheerfully.

"You won't admit, I know, that a man can enjoy fresh rolls once he's already had his ration of bread — to you that's a sin. But I don't count a life without love as living at all," he said, twisting Levin's question to suit himself. "What can I do? That's just how I'm made. And really, it does so little harm to anyone, and it gives me so much pleasure..."
"What — is there something new going on?" Levin asked.

"Yes, my friend, there is! You know the type — women like the ones in Ossian's poems, the kind you see in dreams... Well, sometimes you actually run into women like that in real life... and they're terrifying. A woman, you understand, is the kind of subject that stays perfectly fresh no matter how much you study her."
"Well then, maybe it's better not to study her at all."
"No. Some mathematician once said that the pleasure is in searching for the truth, not in finding it."
Levin listened without a word, and no matter how hard he tried, he couldn't get inside his friend's feelings at all, couldn't understand the appeal of studying women like that.
